title: Training neural networks
text:
What this reading is for
A network architecture is only one part of a learning algorithm. Batch size, learning rate, learning-rate schedule, loss function, preprocessing, and model selection all affect the result. This reading uses one channel-like velocity-profile problem to make those choices concrete. It complements Exercise 2, especially its comparisons of normalization, activations, and physical features.
The examples use PyTorch in the course Python environment. No CFD container, additional dataset, or GPU is needed. The supporting files are training_tools.py and training_strategies_experiments.py. They contain the reusable loop and the experiment definitions. The full, recorded comparisons below were executed on a CPU; they are measurements on this prototype, not claims that one strategy is best for every flow problem.
Before inspecting a comparison, predict what might change and why. Then check the prediction against the curves. A more complicated model or training procedure is useful only if the evidence supports it.

title: Training neural networks
text:
One prototype: channel-like velocity profiles
Let \(\eta=y/\delta\) range from the wall to the channel centerline, with \(\delta=0.5\,\mathrm{m}\), \(\nu=10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\), and \(Re_b=2\delta\bar U/\nu\). We generate 12 profiles for \(0.1\leq\bar U\leq1.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) on 128 wall-normal cells, graded toward the wall. Define
\[
a=\frac{Re_b^{0.8}}{30},\qquad
g(\eta)=\log\!\left[1+a(2\eta-\eta^2)\right],\qquad
u_x(\eta_i)=\bar U\frac{g(\eta_i)}{\sum_j w_jg(\eta_j)},
\]
where \(w_j\) are normalized cell-width weights and \(\sum_jw_j=1\). The velocity is zero at the wall, its wall-normal derivative vanishes at the centerline, and its discrete volume-weighted mean is \(\bar U\). This is an explicitly constructed smooth profile family, not an OpenFOAM solution, Spalding’s relation, or a validated turbulence model. It supplies a reproducible training problem with a steep near-wall gradient and a Reynolds-number dependence.
We learn \((\eta,Re_b)\mapsto u_x\). Unlike the dimensionless target in Exercise 2, this prototype uses dimensional velocity as the target, so the common evaluation metric is directly an RMSE in m/s. The same loop also works with a dimensionless target if the evaluation metric correctly reverses all its transformations.
 
Eight complete profiles are used for training, two for validation, and two interior profiles for testing. The split is fixed before fitting input and target standardizers. Training targets receive small, fixed Gaussian perturbations with standard deviation \(0.002\bar U\); validation and test targets remain clean. This lets us distinguish a training observation from the known synthetic reference.
The robust-loss comparison later adds approximately 5% deliberately corrupted training targets. The underlying problem, scalers, and validation profiles remain unchanged; the corrupted experiment is identified separately from the main comparisons.
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from training_tools import ProfileMLP, Standardizer, evaluate, fit, make_profile_problem

torch.set_num_threads(1)  # Fixed CPU setting for these small examples.
problem = make_profile_problem()
train_data = problem["datasets"]["train"]
validation_data = problem["datasets"]["validation"]
test_data = problem["datasets"]["test"]
print(len(train_data), len(validation_data), len(test_data))  # 1024, 256, 256
The standardizer stores training means and standard deviations. A constant feature is assigned scale one, rather than divided by zero. Save the scalers, feature definitions, and split identifiers with a trained model. Applying BatchNorm or LayerNorm inside a network does not replace this data preparation.

title: Training neural networks
text:
What one update actually means
For a batch \(\mathcal B\) of size \(B\), the mean squared error for a scalar output is
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathcal B}(\theta)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i\in\mathcal B}
\left[f_\theta(x_i)-y_i\right]^2.
\]
One optimizer update uses the gradient of this batch loss. An epoch visits the training dataset once. With \(N\) training samples, an epoch normally contains \(\lceil N/B\rceil\) updates if the final smaller batch is retained.








Strategy
Samples used per update
Consequence




Full batch
All training samples
One update per epoch; the gradient uses the entire current dataset.


Mini-batch
A subset, for example 64
More updates per epoch; gradients depend on which samples are grouped together.


Single-sample stochastic updates
One
High update frequency and substantial sampling variability; incompatible with ordinary training-mode BatchNorm1d on these feature vectors.



An equal-epoch comparison without early stopping holds data exposure approximately fixed but gives smaller batches more optimizer updates. An equal-update comparison without early stopping holds the number of updates fixed but exposes larger batches to more samples. Neither also fixes runtime. For this reason, we record epochs, actual updates, samples seen, and elapsed time. Sampling noise, parameter initialization, and dropout are different sources of variability.
The displayed experiments use equal weight per cell sample; Exercise 2 asks you to state and justify your weighting choice. A graded mesh therefore puts more loss terms near the wall. Cell-volume weighting would define a different objective and must be applied consistently, rather than introduced only when a result looks unfavorable.

title: Training neural networks
text:
A reusable supervised training loop
The loop accepts a model, data loaders, a loss, an optimizer, and optionally a scheduler and common evaluation metric. It does not know the CFD case structure: split profiles and build features before creating loaders. It never receives a test loader.
The essential sequence is:

Set model.train() and iterate over shuffled training batches.
Clear gradients, compute predictions and loss, backpropagate, and update the parameters.
Evaluate the current model with model.eval() and disabled gradient recording.
Record a common validation metric, update the schedule at its specified frequency, and retain a copy of the best model state, including normalization buffers.
Restore the validation-selected state after the training budget or optional early-stopping criterion is reached.

The actual implementation used for the comparisons is shown below. The complete supporting file also defines evaluate, the standardizer, and the model components.
from copy import deepcopy
from time import perf_counter

def fit(model, train_loader, validation_loader, loss_fn, optimizer, *, epochs=100,
        metric_fn=None, scheduler=None, scheduler_interval='epoch',
        max_updates=None, patience=20, device='cpu'):
    """Return validation-selected state and history; never access test data."""
    if patience is not None and patience < 1:
        raise ValueError('patience must be positive')
    if epochs < 1 or (max_updates is not None and max_updates < 1):
        raise ValueError('Training budgets must be positive')
    if scheduler_interval not in ('epoch', 'update', 'validation'):
        raise ValueError('Unknown scheduler interval')
    plateau = isinstance(scheduler, torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau)
    if scheduler is not None and plateau != (scheduler_interval == 'validation'):
        raise ValueError('ReduceLROnPlateau requires validation stepping')
    model.to(device)
    history, best, best_value, stale, updates, samples = [], None, float('inf'), 0, 0, 0
    start = perf_counter()
    for epoch in range(1, epochs + 1):
        model.train()
        online_sum, online_n, lr_first, lr_last = 0., 0, None, None
        for x, y in train_loader:
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
            if len(x) < 2 and any(isinstance(m, nn.BatchNorm1d) for m in model.modules()):
                raise ValueError('BatchNorm training requires at least two samples per batch')
            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            pred = model(x)
            loss = loss_fn(pred, y)
            if loss.ndim or not torch.isfinite(loss):
                raise FloatingPointError('Loss must be a finite scalar mean')
            loss.backward()
            if any(p.grad is not None and not torch.isfinite(p.grad).all() for p in model.parameters()):
                raise FloatingPointError('Non-finite gradient')
            lr_last = optimizer.param_groups[0]['lr']
            lr_first = lr_last if lr_first is None else lr_first
            optimizer.step()
            updates += 1
            samples += len(x)
            online_sum += len(x) * loss.item()
            online_n += len(x)
            if scheduler is not None and scheduler_interval == 'update':
                scheduler.step()
            if max_updates is not None and updates >= max_updates:
                break
        if not online_n:
            raise ValueError('Empty training loader')
        validation = evaluate(model, validation_loader, loss_fn, metric_fn, device)
        # Fixed-order evaluation makes training and validation curves comparable.
        training = evaluate(model, DataLoader(train_loader.dataset, batch_size=1024),
                            loss_fn, metric_fn, device)
        if scheduler is not None:
            if scheduler_interval == 'validation':
                scheduler.step(validation['metric'])
            elif scheduler_interval == 'epoch':
                scheduler.step()
        improved = validation['metric'] < best_value
        if improved:
            best_value, stale = validation['metric'], 0
            best = {'model': deepcopy(model.state_dict()),
                    'optimizer': deepcopy(optimizer.state_dict()),
                    'scheduler': None if scheduler is None else deepcopy(scheduler.state_dict()),
                    'epoch': epoch, 'updates': updates}
        else:
            stale += 1
        history.append({'epoch': epoch, 'updates': updates, 'samples_seen': samples,
                        'online_loss': online_sum / online_n,
                        'train_loss': training['loss'], 'validation_loss': validation['loss'],
                        'train_metric': training['metric'], 'validation_metric': validation['metric'],
                        'lr_first': lr_first, 'lr_last': lr_last,
                        'seconds': perf_counter() - start})
        if (max_updates is not None and updates >= max_updates) or (patience is not None and stale >= patience):
            break
    model.load_state_dict(best['model'])
    model.eval()
    return {'history': history, 'best': best, 'best_validation_metric': best_value}
loss_fn must return a scalar mean over equally weighted samples, with a fixed number of target components for regression. The code aggregates evaluation batches using their sample counts. Averaging the means of unequal-sized batches without those counts would give the small final batch too much weight. The online loss is accumulated while parameters change; the separately recorded training metric is evaluated with the final state of that epoch, in evaluation mode, like the validation metric.
The generic interface handles regression tensors (N, n_features) and (N, n_targets). It also handles classification if the network returns class logits and the caller uses CrossEntropyLoss with integer targets (N,) and a suitable common metric. It is not a complete PINN or reinforcement-learning trainer: those require additional residuals, sampling, or trajectory handling. If you introduce sample or class weights, use aggregation matching that weighted objective rather than assuming the present sample-count average is sufficient.

Minimal use on the prototype
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
torch.manual_seed(11)
train_loader = DataLoader(
    train_data, batch_size=64, shuffle=True,
    generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(1011),
)
validation_loader = DataLoader(validation_data, batch_size=1024)
model = ProfileMLP(width=32, depth=3, activation="silu").to(device)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.003)
velocity_scale = problem["y_scaler"].scale.to(device)

def dimensional_mse(prediction, target):
    return ((prediction - target) * velocity_scale).square().mean()

result = fit(
    model, train_loader, validation_loader, nn.MSELoss(), optimizer,
    epochs=240, metric_fn=dimensional_mse, device=device,
)
validation_rmse = result["best_validation_metric"] ** 0.5
This selects a CUDA GPU when available and otherwise uses the CPU. The model is moved before constructing its optimizer, and the metric scale is placed on the same device. The datasets stay in CPU memory; fit transfers each training and validation batch to device. The recorded comparisons here were executed on CPU.
result["best"] includes model, optimizer, and scheduler states at the selected epoch. For inference, save the model state, architecture settings, and scalers. Exact continuation of a shuffled stochastic run additionally requires random-generator/sampler state and a defined continuation point; the example does not implement an exact restart facility. A checkpoint selected by validation error is also distinct from the last training checkpoint.

title: Training neural networks
section: Controlled comparisons and how to read them
text:
Controlled comparisons and how to read them
The main reference model has three hidden layers of width 32 with SiLU activations, an affine output, batch size 64, Adam with learning rate 0.003, and MSE loss. There is no weight decay. The maximum budget is 240 epochs, with early-stopping patience 20. Each setting is repeated with seeds 11, 22, and 33. Data generation and the profile split are fixed; seed changes affect initialization, shuffling, and stochastic layers.
A shared seed controls a random-number stream; it does not make networks with different parameter layouts start from identical functions. Parameter counts are recorded with the results. These are modest, controlled comparisons with fixed settings, not equally exhaustive tuning of every method.
Curves show clean-validation dimensional RMSE: the solid line is the mean over seeds with recorded evaluations at that point, and the shading spans their minimum and maximum. Curves end when all seeds have stopped; stopped histories are not extended. Values are linearly interpolated between recorded evaluations where needed. It is training-run variation, not a predictive confidence interval. Checkpoints are selected by the common validation metric, not by whichever training loss happens to be numerically smallest. The test profiles are used only after selecting a clean-data configuration by its mean best validation MSE across seeds.

Batch size: compare epochs and updates
 
The two axes tell different stories: one counts optimizer updates, the other counts cumulative data exposure in epoch equivalents. Before early stopping, the maximum is 240 updates for full-batch training and 15,360 for batch size 16. If it learns more slowly per epoch, first separate the number of updates from the quality of each gradient estimate. Small batches can make the path noisier; they do not guarantee better generalization or faster execution.
Validation is recorded at epoch boundaries (including a final partial epoch), so runs have different evaluation spacing on the update axis. Under a fixed-update budget, the number of checkpoint-selection opportunities also differs. Early stopping can also change the realized budget. The results table records actual update ranges and final validation errors separately from the best-checkpoint errors; this is a common maximum-budget comparison, not a guarantee of equal work.
A second comparison allows each run up to 1,600 optimizer updates, subject to the same early-stopping rule. Larger batches then see more training samples, and the number of completed epochs differs:
 
The best-checkpoint ranking changes between the epoch-capped and update-capped comparisons. Early stopping also means that actual update counts can differ within each group. The latter also sees more samples per update. The change in ranking shows why the comparison budget must be stated.


Learning rate: step length matters
The learning rate controls the scale of a parameter update. Too small a rate may leave a model under-trained within the available budget; too large a rate can cause oscillations or divergence. Adam adapts updates per parameter but still needs a sensible global learning rate. A larger network, a different activation, target scaling, and batch size can all change which rate works well.
 
All three rates use the same architecture and 240-epoch budget. A finite but poor curve is a valid outcome, not a reason to remove that run. The helper explicitly raises on non-finite losses or gradients. If a setting diverges, record the failure and change it as a new experiment.


Learning-rate schedules








Schedule
Change rule in this example
When step is called

No scheduler

Schedulers are stepped after the corresponding optimizer work, not before the first optimizer update. ReduceLROnPlateau consumes the validation metric; StepLR and CosineAnnealingLR do not. A per-epoch schedule cannot be compared with a per-update schedule merely by giving their counters the same integer. The PyTorch optimizer documentation describes these interfaces and ordering.
 
 
With these budgets and stopping rules, plateau decay has lower mean best validation error than the constant-rate reference; step and cosine decay give different outcomes. These observations concern the stated rates and budgets; they do not establish a general ranking of schedules.
A decreasing rate can help refine a fit, but reducing it before useful progress has been made can also freeze a poor solution. Plateau scheduling and early stopping serve different purposes: one changes update sizes, while the other terminates training. The default is patience=20: training stops after 20 consecutive validation evaluations without a new best metric. Set patience=None to disable early stopping. Each run has a maximum of 240 epochs (or 1,600 updates in the update-budget comparison), and restores its best validation checkpoint. Scheduler patience is separate and controls learning-rate reductions.
When the epoch cap is reached: if early stopping has not triggered, optimization may still benefit from more epochs, especially if validation error continues to decrease. This is a reason to try a larger budget, not a guarantee of improved generalization. The maximum epoch budget is deliberately kept modest in this educational notebook so the comparisons remain practical to run.


Architecture variants
The model factory makes the modifications explicit. depth=3 means one input-to-hidden layer followed by two hidden blocks, then the affine output.
class HiddenBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, width, normalization, activation, dropout, residual):
        super().__init__()
        norm = {'none': nn.Identity, 'layer': lambda: nn.LayerNorm(width),
                'batch': lambda: nn.BatchNorm1d(width)}[normalization]
        self.branch = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(width, width), norm(), activation(),
                                    nn.Dropout(dropout))
        self.residual = residual

    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.branch(x)
        return x + out if self.residual else out

class ProfileMLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_in=2, n_out=1, width=32, depth=3, normalization='none',
                 residual=False, concatenate=False, dropout=0., activation='silu'):
        super().__init__()
        if depth < 1:
            raise ValueError('depth must be positive')
        act = {'tanh': nn.Tanh, 'relu': nn.ReLU, 'silu': nn.SiLU}[activation]
        self.input = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(n_in, width), act())
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([
            HiddenBlock(width, normalization, act, dropout, residual)
            for _ in range(depth - 1)
        ])
        self.concatenate = concatenate
        self.output = nn.Linear(width + (n_in if concatenate else 0), n_out)

    def forward(self, x):
        h = self.input(x)
        for block in self.blocks:
            h = block(h)
        if self.concatenate:
            h = torch.cat((h, x), dim=-1)
        return self.output(h)








Variant
What changes
What to watch




Plain MLP
Repeated affine maps and activations
A useful reference before adding components.


LayerNorm
Normalize hidden features within each sample, with learned scale and offset
No batch statistics; can still change how scalar information is represented.


BatchNorm
Normalize hidden features using training-batch statistics and retain running statistics for evaluation
Batch composition, small batches, and training/evaluation modes matter.


Additive residual connection
Pass \(h+F(h)\) to the next block
Shapes must match; the implemented width is constant.


Concatenated skip connection
Pass the original input to the output layer alongside the final hidden representation
Unlike addition, concatenation increases the next layer’s input dimension.


Dropout
Randomly zero hidden activations during training, with the module’s scale compensation
Evaluation disables dropout; regularization can underfit a small smooth dataset.



BatchNorm1d uses batch statistics during training and, with the default configuration used here, running statistics in evaluation. LayerNorm uses statistics within each input in both modes. Their behavior is therefore not interchangeable. The helper rejects a singleton training batch when BatchNorm is present; choose a compatible batch partition instead of silently losing samples.
 
The residual variant has the same trainable parameter count as the plain model in this implementation; normalization and concatenated-input variants add parameters. Dropout adds no trainable parameters but changes the training process. None is guaranteed to improve this small regression problem. A fair follow-up would give each architecture a comparable validation-based tuning budget.
Activation functions also matter. The following holds width, depth, normalization, optimizer, and budget fixed while replacing SiLU with tanh or ReLU:
 


Loss functions: what errors should the model emphasize?
For a scalar residual \(r=\hat y-y\), MSE uses \(r^2\), MAE uses \(|r|\), and Huber loss uses
\[
\ell_\delta(r)=
\begin{cases}
\frac12r^2,& |r|\leq\delta,\\
\delta\left(|r|-\frac12\delta\right),& |r|>\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
MSE gives a growing gradient to large residuals. MAE gives a gradient with constant magnitude away from zero. Huber combines a quadratic center with linear tails; it can reduce the influence of large corrupted targets while retaining a smooth central region. These objectives can favor different conditional statistics and should be chosen to match the problem, rather than only to obtain a smaller displayed training number. PyTorch HuberLoss defines the threshold convention used here.
For this comparison, all three losses see the same corrupted training targets: every twentieth scaled target receives an offset of 3. The Huber threshold is 0.2 in standardized target units, corresponding to \(0.2s_y\) m/s, where \(s_y\) is the training target standard deviation. Scalers remain fixed across this controlled corruption experiment. A reference MSE run without outliers appears as a separate clean-data control in the figure.
 
The corrupted-target MSE runs have substantially higher validation error than the MAE and Huber runs here. The clean MSE control separates the effect of target corruption from changing the loss.
The vertical axis is the same clean-validation RMSE in m/s for every loss. Comparing raw MAE, MSE, and Huber values would mix different objectives and scales. Robust losses do not repair physically inconsistent labels, poor mesh resolution, or an unrepresentative dataset. Here the corruption is known because we introduced it; real data require independent quality checks.

Combining training strategies
A strategy that helps on its own need not help in combination: normalization changes the activations seen by later layers, and the schedule changes the optimization path. This comparison tests a small factorial set: LayerNorm with SiLU, tanh, or ReLU, each with constant learning rate 0.003 or validation-based plateau decay. LayerNorm was the strongest individual architecture in the preceding comparison; all three activations are retained rather than assuming the individually best activation remains best with normalization.
All six combinations use the same training-only scalers, profile split, MSE objective, batch size 64, width 32, three hidden layers, a maximum of 240 epochs, and seeds 11, 22, and 33. Plateau decay uses factor 0.5, patience 10, and minimum learning rate 0.00001. The LayerNorm–SiLU–constant configuration reuses the architecture reference. title: Training neural networks
section: Final run: let early stopping decide
text:
Final run: let early stopping decide
The selected LayerNorm + SiLU + validation-based plateau schedule is trained with a generous 50,000-epoch maximum and early-stopping patience 20. title: Surrogate models for continuous predictions
text:
The high Schmidt number problem
The complementary code notebook provides the worked implementation, and the exercise uses it to investigate other bubbles and the limits of the approximation.
This lecture continues our bubble-scale description of gas–liquid mass transfer. In the previous lecture, the surrogate predicted a discrete bubble regime. Here, we want to predict continuous quantities, such as a bubble’s rise velocity, shape, and interfacial velocity. These predictions will help us compute the transport of dissolved gas near the interface.

A thin layer controls the transfer
In the Taylor-bubble example from the previous lecture, the colored reaction product was most clearly visible in the wake. This does not mean that oxygen entered the liquid only at the rear of the bubble: dissolved gas can be transported along the interface inside a layer too thin to see easily. We now look more closely at that layer (Weiner et al. 2021).
We consider a mildly deformed bubble rising through otherwise quiescent liquid. In a reference frame translating with the bubble, its center stays fixed and liquid approaches from above. For a clean, mobile interface, tangential motion also drives circulation inside the gas. The upward arrow in the sketch indicates the bubble’s rise velocity in the laboratory frame; the external streamline arrows indicate the relative liquid motion.
 
Conceptual sketch, not a flow solution. The layer widths are exaggerated and do not reproduce the numerical ratios calculated below. The orange region follows the local concentration layer into the downstream wake between the inner streamlines; the dashed contour represents an effective mean concentration film. The drawn layer edges are not sharp physical boundaries. The actual concentration varies smoothly, and its local layer thickness changes along the interface.
The liquid-sided velocity boundary layer, with characteristic thickness \(\delta_h\), accommodates viscous adjustments to the surrounding flow. At a mobile gas–liquid interface, the tangential velocity can be nonzero. At a stationary no-slip wall, it is zero. Within the much thinner concentration boundary layer, the concentration changes from its interfacial value toward the bulk value.
Near the interface, molecular diffusion supplies dissolved gas in the normal direction, while the liquid flow carries it in the tangential direction. For a steady, thin-layer estimate, the leading balance can be written schematically as
\[
u_t\frac{\partial c}{\partial s}
\sim D_l\frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial n^2},
\]
where \(s\) and \(n\) are tangential and normal coordinates, \(u_t\) is the tangential liquid velocity, and \(D_l\) is the molecular diffusivity. This balance explains why the local layer depends on both diffusion and the flow along the surface. Unsteadiness, interface deformation, and transport into the wake complicate the full problem; they are omitted from this scaling estimate.


Three dimensionless groups
We use the sphere-equivalent bubble diameter \(d_b\), the characteristic rise speed \(U_b\), and the liquid’s kinematic viscosity \(\nu_l\). The Reynolds number compares inertia with viscous forces:
\[
Re=\frac{U_b d_b}{\nu_l}.
\]
The Schmidt number compares the molecular diffusivities of momentum and species:
\[
Sc=\frac{\nu_l}{D_l}.
\]
A large \(Sc\) means that momentum diffuses much more rapidly than the dissolved species. The concentration can therefore vary on much shorter length scales than the velocity.
The Péclet number compares convective and diffusive species transport on the bubble scale:
\[
Pe=\frac{U_b d_b}{D_l}=Re\,Sc.
\]
With lengths scaled by \(d_b\), velocities by \(U_b\), and time by \(d_b/U_b\), the passive-species equation takes the dimensionless form
\[
\frac{\partial c^*}{\partial t^*}
+\mathbf{u}^*\cdot\nabla^*c^*
=\frac{1}{Pe}\nabla^{*2}c^*.
\]
When \(Pe\) is large, diffusion is weak on the bubble scale. It still controls transport across the interface, where the concentration gradients become very steep.


A one-millimeter bubble in water
For an order-of-magnitude example, we use the following approximate water–oxygen properties and rise speed:







Quantity
Value




Bubble diameter \(d_b\)
\(1\,\mathrm{mm}=10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}\)


Rise speed \(U_b\)
\(0.25\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}=25\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\)


Kinematic liquid viscosity \(\nu_l\)
\(10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\)


Dissolved-oxygen diffusivity \(D_l\)
\(2\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\)



These are illustrative inputs, rather than a prediction of the terminal speed for every one-millimeter bubble. In particular, interfacial contamination can change the rise speed and surface mobility. With these inputs, we obtain
\[
Re=\frac{0.25\times10^{-3}}{10^{-6}}=250,
\qquad
Sc=\frac{10^{-6}}{2\times10^{-9}}=500,
\]
and therefore
\[Pe=250\times500=1.25\times10^5\approx10^5.\]


From dimensionless groups to layer thicknesses
We use classical clean-bubble estimates to put physical dimensions on these numbers. The hydrodynamic thickness estimate quoted by Weiner and Bothe (2017), with reference to p. 441 of Levich (1962), is
\[
\frac{\delta_h}{d_b}\approx\frac{1}{\sqrt{2Re}},
\qquad
\frac{d_b}{\delta_h}\approx\sqrt{2Re}.
\]
For our example,
\[
\frac{d_b}{\delta_h}\approx\sqrt{500}\approx22.4,
\qquad
\delta_h\approx\frac{1\,\mathrm{mm}}{22.4}
\approx44.7\,\mu\mathrm{m}.
\]
The velocity layer is already more than twenty times thinner than the bubble diameter. To estimate the concentration layer, we introduce an effective mean film thickness \(\overline{\delta}_c\). In film theory, the mean liquid-side transfer coefficient is \(k_L=D_l/\overline{\delta}_c\), so the Sherwood number is \(Sh=k_Ld_b/D_l=d_b/\overline{\delta}_c\). The classical high-\(Pe\), clean-bubble estimate \(Sh\approx2\sqrt{Pe/\pi}\) then gives (Weiner and Bothe 2017)
\[
\frac{\overline{\delta}_c}{d_b}
\approx\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2\sqrt{Pe}},
\qquad
\frac{\overline{\delta}_c}{\delta_h}
\approx\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2Sc}}.
\]
Equivalently, the velocity layer is thicker by a factor
\[
\frac{\delta_h}{\overline{\delta}_c}
\approx\sqrt{\frac{2Sc}{\pi}}
=\sqrt{\frac{1000}{\pi}}\approx17.8.
\]
Thus,
\[
\overline{\delta}_c\approx\frac{44.7\,\mu\mathrm{m}}{17.8}
\approx2.51\,\mu\mathrm{m},
\qquad
\frac{d_b}{\overline{\delta}_c}\approx400.
\]
This effective film reproduces a mean mass-transfer rate; it is not the arithmetic average of a sharply defined local layer edge. The dashed contour in the sketch represents this simplification. The estimates assume a clean, mobile interface and idealized flow; deformation, finite-\(Re\) corrections, surfactants, and reactions can alter the prefactors or the scaling. Here, their purpose is to explain the separation of scales.


Why numerical resolution becomes expensive
As a practical starting estimate, we ask for at least ten cells across the concentration boundary layer. Using the mean thickness above, the interface-normal cell width would need to satisfy approximately
\[
\Delta n\lesssim\frac{\overline{\delta}_c}{10}
\approx0.25\,\mu\mathrm{m},
\qquad
\frac{d_b}{\Delta n}\gtrsim4000.
\]
The second number expresses an equivalent uniform resolution across one bubble diameter. It is not the total cell count of an adaptively refined or interface-aligned mesh. Moreover, ten cells is a planning rule, not a proof of accuracy: the thinnest local layers may require smaller cells, and mass-transfer rates must be checked by mesh refinement.

title: Surrogate models for continuous predictions
text:
The sharp-interface flow model

Two domains and one moving interface
A common mathematical model describes the liquid and gas phases as separate time-dependent domains,
\[
\Omega^+(t)\quad\text{(liquid)},
\qquad
\Omega^-(t)\quad\text{(gas)},
\]
with a common interface \(\Sigma(t)\). Throughout this lecture, the unit normal \(\mathbf{n}_\Sigma\) points from \(\Omega^-\) into \(\Omega^+\), hence from the gas into the liquid. This choice fixes the signs of all jump conditions below.
 
Conceptual sharp-interface model. Each phase has its own balance equations, and transmission conditions couple their one-sided values at the moving interface.
The word sharp means that the phase transition is represented by a surface of zero geometric thickness. In the model used here, we also assume that this surface carries no stored mass, so there is no separate interfacial mass inventory. These are distinct modeling choices: more general sharp-interface models can include adsorbed interfacial mass (Bothe 2022). A massless interface can nevertheless exert a surface-tension force.
We therefore have two sets of bulk balance equations, one in each domain, together with kinematic and dynamic coupling conditions on \(\Sigma(t)\). The sketch shows the incompressible mass and momentum balances, with \(\mathrm{D}/\mathrm{D}t\) denoting the material derivative and \(\mathbf{g}\) gravity. We focus below on the interface conditions that a second simulation must reproduce.


Slow dissolution and the normal velocity
The relevant separation of time scales is
\[
\tau_{\mathrm{BL}}\ll\tau_{\mathrm{size}},
\qquad
\tau_{\mathrm{size}}\sim\frac{d_b}{|\mathrm{d}d_b/\mathrm{d}t|},
\]
where \(\tau_{\mathrm{BL}}\) characterizes development of the concentration boundary layer and \(\tau_{\mathrm{size}}\) characterizes the diameter change caused by dissolution. Over the time needed to establish the boundary layer, the bubble then loses only a small fraction of its volume. We can investigate different bubble sizes and Reynolds numbers separately, retaining species transfer while neglecting its feedback through shrinkage. Hydrodynamic deformation is still allowed; neglecting dissolution-induced volume change does not require a fixed shape.
To state the condition precisely, we denote the local interface velocity by \(\mathbf{u}_\Sigma\) and its normal component by \(V_\Sigma=\mathbf{u}_\Sigma\cdot\mathbf{n}_\Sigma\). The one-sided total mass fluxes per unit area, measured relative to that moving surface, are
\[
\dot m^\pm
=\rho^\pm\left(\mathbf{u}^\pm-\mathbf{u}_\Sigma\right)
\cdot\mathbf{n}_\Sigma.
\]
Without interfacial mass accumulation, conservation gives
\[
\dot m^+-\dot m^-=0
\qquad\text{on }\Sigma(t).
\]
Equal mass fluxes alone do not imply equal normal velocities when the densities differ. In our leading-order hydrodynamic approximation, we additionally neglect the total mass crossing the interface and set \(\dot m^+=\dot m^-=0\). Consequently,
\[
\mathbf{u}^+\cdot\mathbf{n}_\Sigma
=\mathbf{u}^-\cdot\mathbf{n}_\Sigma
=V_\Sigma.
\]
The interface moves with the fluid in the normal direction. The much slower loss of gas is omitted from this hydrodynamic problem, while its dissolved concentration and transfer rate remain the quantities of interest in the species calculation. This is a one-way approximation, not an exact description of a shrinking bubble.


Tangential continuity is a closure assumption
We also assume that the two fluids do not slip tangentially relative to one another at the interface. With the tangential projector
\[
\mathbf{P}_\Sigma=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{n}_\Sigma\otimes\mathbf{n}_\Sigma,
\]
the condition reads
\[
\mathbf{P}_\Sigma\mathbf{u}^+
=\mathbf{P}_\Sigma\mathbf{u}^-
\qquad\text{on }\Sigma(t).
\]
This is an interfacial constitutive assumption, not a consequence of mass conservation. Combined with the normal-velocity condition, it gives continuity of the full velocity trace:
\[\mathbf{u}^+=\mathbf{u}^-\qquad\text{on }\Sigma(t).\]
Continuity does not mean that the tangential velocity is zero. Both phases can move along the interface, as in the recirculating bubble sketch. A shear-free approximation would concern the tangential traction, not the tangential velocity.


Momentum transmission and surface tension
Velocity continuity is accompanied by a force balance. We define the Newtonian Cauchy stress and our jump convention as
\[
\mathbf{T}^\pm=-p^\pm\mathbf{I}
+\mu^\pm\left[\nabla\mathbf{u}^\pm+
\left(\nabla\mathbf{u}^\pm\right)^{\mathsf T}\right],
\qquad
[\![a]\!]=a^+ - a^-.
\]
Here, \(\mu^\pm\) are the dynamic viscosities. For the massless interface with no total mass crossing it, the momentum transmission condition is
\[
[\![\mathbf{T}]\!]\mathbf{n}_\Sigma
=\gamma\kappa\mathbf{n}_\Sigma-\nabla_\Sigma\gamma,
\qquad
\kappa=\nabla_\Sigma\cdot\mathbf{n}_\Sigma,
\]
where \(\gamma\) is the surface tension and \(\nabla_\Sigma\) denotes the surface gradient. For a clean interface with constant \(\gamma\), the gradient term vanishes: the normal traction jump balances capillarity, and tangential traction is continuous. For varying surface tension, the tangential term represents Marangoni forcing.
Writing \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^\pm=\mathbf T^\pm+p^\pm\mathbf I\) for the viscous stress, we can project the jump onto the normal and tangent plane:
\[
p^- - p^+ + \mathbf n_\Sigma\cdot[\![\boldsymbol{\tau}]\!]\mathbf n_\Sigma
=\gamma\kappa,
\qquad
\mathbf P_\Sigma[\![\boldsymbol{\tau}]\!]\mathbf n_\Sigma
=-\nabla_\Sigma\gamma.
\]
The normal equation relates the pressure values at the interface. Pressure drops out of the tangential equation, which governs the viscous shear jump. Neither projection specifies the liquid-side normal pressure derivative used in the liquid-only simulation.
A static spherical bubble checks the signs: our normal points outward, so \(\kappa=2/R\). With zero viscous stress, the condition gives the familiar pressure difference
\[p^- - p^+=\frac{2\gamma}{R}.\]
The gas pressure is larger even though velocity is continuous. In the hybrid simulation, the learned interface motion and surface velocity must therefore be compatible with a flow solution; prescribing only a bubble outline would leave essential coupling information out.

title: Surrogate models for continuous predictions
section: Two numerical representations of the interface
text:
Two numerical representations of the interface
The sharp-interface model describes the physics. We still need a numerical representation of its moving domains. Two useful choices make the motivation for our hybrid approach clearer.

Volume of fluid: the interface cuts through bulk cells
In the volume-of-fluid (VOF) representation, we first define a gas-phase indicator (Hirt and Nichols 1981):
\[
\chi_g(\mathbf{x},t)=
\begin{cases}
1,&\mathbf{x}\in\Omega^-(t),\\
0,&\mathbf{x}\in\Omega^+(t).
\end{cases}
\]
The value directly on the zero-thickness interface does not affect a volume integral. For a computational cell \(K\), the stored gas volume fraction is the cell average of this indicator:
\[
\alpha_{g,K}(t)
=\frac{1}{|K|}\int_K\chi_g(\mathbf{x},t)\,\mathrm{d}V
=\frac{|K\cap\Omega^-(t)|}{|K|}.
\]
Pure liquid cells have \(\alpha_{g,K}=0\), pure gas cells have \(\alpha_{g,K}=1\), and cut cells have \(0<\alpha_{g,K}<1\). The intermediate value describes how much gas occupies a cell; it is not a locally mixed physical phase.
 
Conceptual two-dimensional geometric VOF representation. Color indicates the gas volume fraction; the segments reconstruct an interface inside cut cells. In this planar illustration, area fractions play the role of volume fractions.
The interface is represented implicitly by the collection of volume fractions. A geometric reconstruction additionally estimates its orientation and places a line segment in each cut cell so that the reconstructed gas area matches the stored fraction. In three dimensions, a plane replaces that line. This is the idea of piecewise linear interface calculation (PLIC). A fraction alone does not uniquely determine a segment: neighboring data and a normal-estimation procedure are needed (Roenby et al. 2016).
VOF is attractive for robust, comparatively efficient simulations of moving and strongly deforming interfaces on bulk meshes. It also accommodates topology changes without maintaining a fitted boundary mesh. For our transport problem, however, the cell faces generally do not follow the interface. Accurately resolving a steep concentration gradient normal to that interface, and advecting the thin layer along it, can therefore demand substantial local refinement or a subgrid model.
This is a limitation of the mesh–interface relationship and transport discretization, rather than a statement that all VOF schemes have poor accuracy. Geometric reconstruction and advection can be highly accurate; a coarse PLIC description alone does not resolve a micrometer-scale concentration layer.


Interface tracking: the mesh follows the phase boundary
Here, interface tracking means an interface-fitted moving-mesh approach. The liquid and gas occupy separate mesh regions, and their shared boundary explicitly represents \(\Sigma(t)\). Mesh faces on that boundary move with the interface; interior points move to maintain mesh quality (Tuković and Jasak 2012).
 
Conceptual interface-fitted mesh. The shared boundary is an actual mesh boundary, and liquid cells can be thin in the normal direction while remaining longer along the surface. The drawing is not a convergence-tested simulation mesh.
This representation is especially useful for an isolated bubble with moderate deformation. Transmission conditions can be applied directly at boundary faces, and interface-aligned cell layers give precise control over the normal resolution needed for mass transfer. It is therefore well suited to high-accuracy interfacial transport calculations.
The cost is additional geometric and algorithmic work: mesh motion, iterative phase coupling, and possibly remeshing. Large deformations can degrade cells and threaten robustness; breakup and coalescence are much harder to accommodate than in VOF. Its accuracy and runtime still depend on the implementation and mesh, rather than on the method name alone.


Why combine these ideas?








Representation
Useful feature for this lecture
Main difficulty for this lecture




VOF on a bulk mesh
Efficient, robust generation of bubble motion and deformation data
Very thin interfacial concentration layers need extra resolution or modeling


Interface-fitted moving mesh
Direct boundary conditions and concentrated interface-normal resolution
Maintaining two moving, coupled phase meshes adds complexity



We would like to retain the practical two-phase flow calculation while exploiting an interface-aligned liquid mesh for the expensive species problem. The continuous surrogate models connect those two representations.

title: Surrogate models for continuous predictions
text:
A simplified simulation approach
We now combine the practical strengths of the two representations: VOF provides the bubble dynamics, while a surface-aligned liquid mesh provides the resolution for species transport. The information passed between them consists of continuous functions learned from the first simulation. The strategy follows Section 2.3 of Weiner et al. (2022). In this lecture, the first-stage data come from VOF; the reference study used a front-tracking solver for that stage.

Four steps from two-phase flow to resolved species transport
 
Conceptual workflow. The regression curves and concentration wake are illustrative.
At each saved VOF time, we obtain the rise speed from the bubble-center history and sample positions and liquid velocities on the reconstructed interface. In the translating bubble frame, those samples give the radius \(r\) and the tangential velocity \(u_t\) as functions of polar angle. The fitted rise speed sets the inflow, while the fitted radius and tangential velocity set the moving boundary and its velocity. The liquid solver then computes the transient flow and species transport.
In the liquid-only case, the surrogate prescribes the moving interface and its velocity. OpenFOAM solves for the liquid kinematic pressure \(p/\rho^+\) with a homogeneous Neumann condition at the bubble, \(\partial_{n_\Sigma}(p/\rho^+)=0\), and a pressure reference at the outlet. This extrapolates the liquid pressure to the bubble with zero normal slope, while allowing it to vary along the surface. The normal component of the liquid momentum equation can give a nonzero pressure gradient when acceleration, viscosity, or body forces contribute. Even quasi-steady tangential flow can have normal acceleration as it follows the curved surface.


Parameterizing an axisymmetric bubble
We assume a straight rise path, azimuthal symmetry of shape and flow, and no azimuthal swirl. The calculation is performed in a meridional section, but represents a three-dimensional body of revolution. It is therefore an axisymmetric simulation, rather than a planar two-dimensional bubble.
The polar angle \(\vartheta\in[0,\pi]\) is measured from the upward rise axis: \(\vartheta=0\) is the front pole and \(\vartheta=\pi\) is the rear pole. The azimuthal angle is \(\varphi\), and \(\mathbf{e}_r(\vartheta,\varphi)\) is the radial unit vector. Relative to the bubble center \(\mathbf{x}_b(t)\), we parameterize the surface by
\[
\mathbf{x}_\Sigma(t,\vartheta,\varphi)
=\mathbf{x}_b(t)+r(t,\vartheta)\mathbf{e}_r(\vartheta,\varphi),
\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_b}{\mathrm{d}t}=U_b(t)\mathbf{e}_z.
\]
This radius representation requires a single surface intersection along each ray from the center. It is suitable for the mildly deformed bubbles considered here; it does not describe arbitrary overhanging or breaking interfaces.
 
Conceptual meridional geometry. The tangent points toward increasing polar angle, and the normal retains our gas-to-liquid orientation. Surface motion and fluid motion have the same normal component in the approximation used here; their tangential components need not coincide.


Which velocity do we learn?
We subtract the translational velocity of the bubble center from the laboratory-frame liquid velocity:
\[
\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{rel}}\big|_\Sigma
=\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{lab}}\big|_\Sigma-U_b(t)\mathbf{e}_z.
\]
With \(\mathbf{t}_\Sigma\) the unit tangent toward increasing \(\vartheta\), its two meridional components are
\[
u_t=\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{rel}}\big|_\Sigma\cdot\mathbf{t}_\Sigma,
\qquad
u_n=\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{rel}}\big|_\Sigma\cdot\mathbf{n}_\Sigma.
\]
We learn \(u_t\) in the translating frame, rather than a laboratory-frame tangential component or the difference between fluid velocity and the full local mesh velocity. Translation and deformation are separate: after subtracting the rise speed, the bubble can still deform.
Interface positions provide the training data for \(r(t,\vartheta)\). They are generally easier to extract reliably than a small normal velocity obtained by projecting a reconstructed interfacial flow field. Differentiating the learned radius also ensures that the prescribed normal motion and boundary velocity refer to the same predicted surface.


Regression forms that enforce known structure
The networks \(f_U\), \(f_r\), and \(f_t\) use the normalized time \(q(t)\). We define \(q(t)\) and the startup factor \(s(t)\) using dimensionless time \(t\) and the last available snapshot time \(T\).
\[
q(t)=\frac{\log(1+t)}{\log(1+T)},\qquad
s(t)=\frac{t}{1+t}.
\]
The predictions used in the worked example are
\[
\boxed{\widehat U_b(t)=S_U\,s(t)f_U\!\left(q(t)\right)}
\]
\[
\boxed{\widehat r(t,\vartheta)
=r_0+S_r\,s(t)^2f_r\!\left(q(t),\cos(\vartheta)\right)}
\]
\[
\boxed{\widehat u_t(t,\vartheta)
=S_t\,s(t)\sin(\vartheta)f_t\!\left(q(t),\cos(\vartheta)\right)}.
\]
Here, \(r_0\) is the initial spherical radius. The output scales \(S_U\), \(S_r\), and \(S_t\) are determined from the training targets. The startup and angular factors enforce the following constraints.

Initial rise speed: \(\widehat{U}_b(0)=0\) for a finite network output.
Initial shape: \(\widehat{r}(0,\vartheta)=r_0\) at every angle. The squared startup factor also gives \(\partial_t\widehat r(0,\vartheta)=0\).
Shape symmetry: because \(\cos(-\vartheta)=\cos(\vartheta)\), a full-meridian extension satisfies \(\widehat{r}(t,-\vartheta)=\widehat{r}(t,\vartheta)\). It is also \(2\pi\)-periodic. For a differentiable model, the angular radius derivative vanishes at both poles.
Tangential antisymmetry and regularity: the sine factor gives \(\widehat{u}_t(t,-\vartheta)=-\widehat{u}_t(t,\vartheta)\) in the signed full-meridian extension. On the physical interval \([0,\pi]\), it makes the tangential velocity vanish at both poles. The time factor also gives \(\widehat{u}_t(0,\vartheta)=0\).

These are reflection symmetries about the rise axis. They do not force the front and rear of the bubble to have identical shapes or velocities: \(\cos(0)=1\) and \(\cos(\pi)=-1\) remain distinct network inputs.
A positive radius and constant bubble volume still require checks when fitting the shape.
We fit the constrained predictions directly to the observed quantities, avoiding division by the startup or sine factors where they vanish.


From the learned radius to mesh motion and normal velocity
We differentiate the radius at fixed polar angle, so \(z=\cos(\vartheta)\) is constant.
\[
\partial_t\widehat r
= S_r\left[
2s(t)s'(t)f_r\!\left(q(t),z\right)
+s(t)^2q'(t)\,\partial_q f_r\!\left(q(t),z\right)
\right].
\]
Here, \(s'(t)=1/(1+t)^2\) and \(q'(t)=1/[(1+t)\log(1+T)]\).
In bubble-fixed coordinates, a boundary point at fixed \((\vartheta,\varphi)\) moves radially with
\[
\mathbf{w}_\Sigma
=\frac{\partial\widehat r}{\partial t}\mathbf{e}_r.
\]
Its normal component determines the fluid’s normal boundary velocity. The prescribed liquid velocity is therefore
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{rel}}\big|_\Sigma
=\widehat{u}_t\mathbf{t}_\Sigma
+\left(\frac{\partial\widehat r}{\partial t}
\mathbf{e}_r\cdot\mathbf{n}_\Sigma\right)\mathbf{n}_\Sigma
}.
\]
The projection is important: on a deformed bubble, radial and normal directions generally differ. In particular, \(\partial_t\widehat r\) is not itself the signed normal speed. With \(\widehat r_\vartheta=\partial\widehat r/\partial\vartheta\), our gas-to-liquid normal satisfies
\[
\mathbf{n}_\Sigma
=\frac{\widehat r\mathbf{e}_r-\widehat r_\vartheta\mathbf{e}_\vartheta}
{\sqrt{\widehat r^2+\widehat r_\vartheta^2}},
\qquad
\widehat{u}_n
=\frac{\widehat r\,\partial_t\widehat r}
{\sqrt{\widehat r^2+\widehat r_\vartheta^2}}.
\]
The same predicted radius sets the displacement of an initially spherical boundary,
\[
\Delta\mathbf{x}_\Sigma
=\left[\widehat r(t,\vartheta)-r_0\right]\mathbf{e}_r.
\]
We can evaluate the time derivative analytically, by automatic differentiation, or consistently from successive predicted boundary positions. A time-discrete implementation uses the same boundary positions for mesh motion and its normal-velocity condition, so two independently fitted approximations cannot contradict one another. The mesh may move radially while the fluid moves tangentially along it; only their normal components must agree.


Inflow and transient species transport
The undisturbed liquid is at rest in the laboratory frame. It therefore enters the translating-frame calculation with the time-dependent velocity
\[
\boxed{\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{in}}(t)
=-\widehat U_b(t)\mathbf{e}_z}.
\]
The inner boundary receives the displacement and velocity conditions above, and the liquid solver computes the flow throughout the remaining domain. If the frame accelerates, its acceleration must also be treated consistently in the momentum/pressure formulation; changing the inlet velocity alone does not specify a complete non-inertial formulation.
We then use that transient flow to compute the dissolved-species concentration, for example with a prescribed equilibrium concentration at the bubble boundary and a lower concentration in the incoming liquid. The fine, interface-aligned cells are used where the normal concentration gradient is steep. A moving-mesh solver accounts for mesh motion in its transport fluxes.
The result is a hybrid simulation, with the flow boundary data represented by regression models and the liquid flow and species fields still obtained from conservation equations. We preserve the time dependence of the original bubble dynamics while concentrating the spatial resolution on the liquid-side transport problem.


Computed deformation and concentration transport
The animations show OpenFOAM fields from the AOTInductor and LibTorch workflow. The three panels have the same bubble and velocity field at each time: only the diffusion coefficient changes, giving \(Sc=100\), \(1000\), and \(10000\). The Reynolds number varies during startup, with \(Re(t)=Ga\,\widehat U_b(t)\) and \(Ga=238.2\) in this dimensionless case.






Actual cell-associated concentration, on a common fixed scale from 0 to 1. This near-bubble meridional view is reflected by axisymmetry. The interface outline follows the moving mesh; the gas interior is excluded from the liquid calculation.






Actual mesh cells, with a close-up following the interface near a polar angle of \(45^\circ\). The local axes are tangential distance \(s\) and outward normal distance \(n\); the view translates and rotates, without stretching the geometry. Cell colors show \(Sc=1000\), with no cell-to-point smoothing.
The animations use 200 saved snapshots from \(0.05\leq\tilde t\leq10\) on a 13,584-cell mesh with 132 faces along the bubble and milder interface-normal grading. The mesh close-up shows that the steep concentration change at \(Sc=1000\) occupies only a few cells normal to the interface. The layer is thinner still at \(Sc=10000\). This limited resolution makes the interfacial gradient and Sherwood numbers sensitive to mesh spacing. A refinement study is needed to establish mesh convergence.

title: Surrogate models for discrete predictions
text:
Aim of the exercise
The lecture developed a classifier from digitized numerical observations. The central question of this exercise is: How much can we improve the robustness and accuracy of this classifier based on additional numerical or experimental data?
Investigate the lecture data from Tripathi et al. (2015) alongside experimental observations from Sharaf et al. (2017). Inspect the two sources, decide how to represent their labels consistently, and examine how validation performance changes as the training dataset grows.

title: Surrogate models for discrete predictions
text:
Part 1 — Theory

Features and physical conventions

What physical effects do the Galilei and Eötvös numbers compare? If one study defines them using the bubble radius and another uses the diameter, how do the numerical values change for the same bubble?
Explain what the logarithm and the min–max scaling each do to the features. Why do we fit the scaling bounds on the training data? What happens to a validation feature outside those bounds?



Class probabilities and cross entropy

Suppose three logits are \((0,\log(2),\log(4))\). Compute their softmax probabilities and identify the predicted class.
If the true class is the second one, compute the categorical cross entropy. Multiply all three logits by two and repeat. How can the predicted class stay the same while the loss changes?



Labels and validation

Two studies use different names for partly overlapping bubble paths. What evidence would justify merging their labels? When would we leave observations out of the comparison?
Why do we keep related observations together when splitting the data? Explain why the validation cases should stay fixed while we vary the training-set size or network architecture.

title: Surrogate models for discrete predictions
text:
Part 2 — Practical exercise

Files and preparation
Download exercise source Download supplied helpers Download Tripathi data Download Sharaf data
The helpers also use figure_style.py and figure_utils.py. Outside a repository clone, place these three helper files beside the exercise source and save the two CSVs as tripathi2015-points.csv and sharaf2017-points.csv. The code runs locally in Python, not on this HTML page. Run the code blocks in sequence in a Python editor, or open the source as a notebook using Jupytext. NumPy and Matplotlib are needed; figure exports use LaTeX by default. An explicit use_tex=False option is available when TeX is unavailable.

Getting started with the supplied code
The supplied code is our starting point for experimenting: we do not need to implement a classifier or training loop from scratch. The main aim is to run comparisons, try different configurations, and interpret what changes when we vary the data, training-set size, or network architecture.

Download the exercise source, the three helper files linked above, and both CSV files into one working folder. Use the filenames tripathi2015-points.csv and sharaf2017-points.csv for the data.
Run Python from that folder. With these filenames, the supplied dataset_file function finds the data automatically. If the CSVs are stored elsewhere, replace the paths in its choices list with the paths to your local files.
Run the loading block below first and inspect its printed summary. Before training, complete label_maps and class_names in “A common classification problem” after comparing the source labels. These are the intended data-definition choices; the remaining training and plotting code can be used as supplied.
Run the remaining blocks in order to obtain a baseline. Then change one setting at a time, such as the training fractions, network widths and depths, or learning rate, and compare the results using the same validation cases. Keep a record of the settings and explain the observed differences.




Load and investigate the two datasets
The lecture dataset contains 104 digitized markers from Figure 1 of Tripathi et al. (2015). The additional CSV contains 183 discernible markers from the experimental Figure 4 of Sharaf et al. (2017). Their positions were extracted from the embedded high-resolution image and calibrated using the logarithmic axis ticks. Touching and partly obscured markers were reviewed visually. These are approximate digitized coordinates, not the authors’ original raw observations; repeated experiments and fully hidden markers cannot be recovered from the map.
The Tripathi extraction notes and Sharaf extraction notes document the sources and methods. The Sharaf extraction overlay allows the recovered positions to be checked against the publication.

Load both files and inspect their column names, parameter ranges, and class counts.
Plot the two datasets using logarithmic Ga and Eo axes. Make the sources distinguishable and retain their original labels initially.
Compare the marker legends and descriptions in the two papers. Do the same category identifiers describe the same physical behavior? Can every source label be translated unambiguously into the lecture’s classes?
Check the definitions of Ga and Eo, the length scale, and the density and viscosity ratios. Which differences might affect the comparison even after the labels are reconciled?


from pathlib import Path
from collections import Counter
import csv
import json
import numpy as np
from classification_exercise_tools import (
    split_by_source_and_class, learning_curve, save_learning_curve,
    compare_architectures, save_architecture_comparison,
)


def dataset_file(study):
    choices = [Path(f"{study}-points.csv"),
               Path(f"../datasets/path_shape_regimes/{study}_digitization/points.csv"),
               Path(f"datasets/path_shape_regimes/{study}_digitization/points.csv")]
    return next(p for p in choices if p.is_file())


def read_source(study, label_column):
    with dataset_file(study).open(newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as stream:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(stream))
    for row in rows:
        row["Ga"], row["Eo"] = float(row["Ga"]), float(row["Eo"])
        row["source_id"] = study
        row["source_regime"] = row[label_column]
        row["group_id"] = row["point_id"]
    return rows


tripathi = read_source("tripathi2015", "regime")
sharaf = read_source("sharaf2017", "source_regime")
for name, rows in [("Tripathi", tripathi), ("Sharaf", sharaf)]:
    print(name, len(rows), Counter(r["source_regime"] for r in rows))
    print("Columns:", list(rows[0]))
    print("Ga range:", min(r["Ga"] for r in rows), max(r["Ga"] for r in rows))
    print("Eo range:", min(r["Eo"] for r in rows), max(r["Eo"] for r in rows))
    print(rows[:2])



A common classification problem
Before pooling the observations, define a common prediction target. Record and justify the chosen definition in the data-source documentation template.

Explain any differences between the source classifications. Propose a set of classes that can be supported by both datasets and justify any aggregation or exclusion.
Complete the two mapping dictionaries below. Each original label maps to a chosen common class name, or to None if those observations must be excluded. Retain the original labels and document the reasons for exclusions. No new subtype should be inferred solely from a marker’s location.
Compare the retained class counts and parameter coverage. Is the resulting prediction task still exactly the same as in the lecture?

Matching definitions and labels does not establish that Ga and Eo alone explain both sources. Density and viscosity ratios, release conditions, or other unmodeled differences may cause conflicting observations. Keep the source IDs so that such differences remain visible.

# Complete these after investigating the source descriptions.
label_maps = {"tripathi2015": None, "sharaf2017": None}
class_names = None  # Ordered list of the chosen common class names.

if class_names is None or any(v is None for v in label_maps.values()):
    raise ValueError("Choose and document the common classes and both label mappings first")
if len(class_names) < 2 or len(set(class_names)) != len(class_names):
    raise ValueError("At least two distinct common classes are needed")

merged, excluded = [], []
for row in tripathi + sharaf:
    mapping = label_maps[row["source_id"]]
    common_label = mapping[row["source_regime"]]
    if common_label is None:
        excluded.append(dict(row))
    elif common_label in class_names:
        merged.append(dict(row, regime=common_label))
    else:
        raise ValueError("A mapped label is missing from class_names")
print("Retained:", Counter((r["source_id"], r["regime"]) for r in merged))
print("Excluded:", len(excluded))



Merge, then split into training and validation data
Split the harmonized, merged dataset once into approximately 80% training and 20% validation observations. The split preserves representation by source and common class, and related observations remain in the same partition. There is no test set. Each CSV row represents a recoverable marker; the original repeated experiments cannot be reconstructed from the published images.

Run the split below and inspect class and source counts in both partitions. Confirm that no source/case group crosses the split.
Keep the validation cases unchanged throughout the training-size comparison. Adding validation cases as the training set grows would change the quantity being compared.


training, validation = split_by_source_and_class(merged, seed=42)
training_groups = {(merged[i]["source_id"], merged[i]["group_id"]) for i in training}
validation_groups = {(merged[i]["source_id"], merged[i]["group_id"]) for i in validation}
assert not training_groups & validation_groups
for name, indices in [("Training", training), ("Validation", validation)]:
    print(name, len(indices), Counter((merged[i]["source_id"], merged[i]["regime"])
                                     for i in indices))



Validation performance as the training dataset grows
Train the same MLP on increasingly large, nested subsets of the training pool: approximately 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100%. Subsets retain representation by source and common class; their actual sizes depend on rounding and case grouping. For each random seed, all observations in a smaller subset also occur in the larger subsets. Use a smaller network than the lecture’s two-hidden-layer demonstration to keep the repeated fits inexpensive: one hidden layer with 16 tanh units and one softmax output per chosen common class. The classification model, loss, and preprocessing follow the same principles. In the code, common class names are represented by zero-based indices 0,...,K-1; these are identifiers, corresponding to the lecture’s mathematical indices 1,...,K.
Logarithmic min–max scaling is fitted separately on each training subset. The corresponding transformation is reused for the fixed validation set; validation observations never contribute to the scaling or weight updates. Use full-batch Adam with learning rate 0.01, at most 500 epochs, and early-stopping patience 100. Restore the best-validation weights. Repeating the experiment with three seeds shows sensitivity to subset selection and initialization; these repetitions are not independent validation datasets or confidence intervals.

Run the training-size comparison and plot validation cross entropy against the actual number of training points. Also inspect validation accuracy.
Does validation loss decrease as the number of training points increases? Is that trend monotonic and consistent across seeds?
Does accuracy tell the same story as cross entropy? Where might differences between the physical investigations limit the benefit of additional data?
Does this experiment isolate the benefit of Sharaf’s data specifically, or the effect of training size in the pooled dataset? Explain the distinction.


configuration = dict(width=16, learning_rate=0.01, epochs=500, patience=100)
results = learning_curve(merged, training, validation, class_names,
                         fractions=(.2, .4, .6, .8, 1.), seeds=(11, 22, 33),
                         **configuration)
output = Path("output/bubble-classification")
paths = save_learning_curve(output, results, use_tex=True)
for result in results:
    print(result["seed"], result["training_samples"],
          result["validation_cross_entropy"], result["validation_accuracy"])
print("Figures:", paths)

The generated learning-curve-light.svg and learning-curve-dark.svg show validation cross entropy and accuracy against training size. A falling loss would support improved probability predictions on this fixed validation subset; improvement is not guaranteed. The validation set selects early-stopping checkpoints and is reused across runs, so its score is not an independent final test score. It also does not establish robustness to an unseen fluid system or investigation.


Network width, depth, and overfitting
Keep the entire training pool, the validation cases, and the training-fitted scaler fixed. Vary the number of hidden units and hidden layers: (8,), (16,), and (32,) describe one hidden layer; (16,16) and (16,16,16) add one or two more hidden layers. Also test two hidden layers with 32 neurons each. All hidden layers use tanh, and the softmax output still has one unit per common class.
For this diagnostic comparison, all models train for the same 2,000 epochs without a patience-based stopping trigger. Retain the complete training and validation loss histories, the parameters at the validation minimum, and the final parameters. Use these records to examine what happens after validation performance stops improving. The final model and validation-selected model are reported separately.

Compare the networks using the same learning rate, split, and initialization seeds. Record the number of trainable parameters alongside width and depth.
Plot validation accuracy for both the selected and final models. Does a larger network consistently improve accuracy across the seeds?
Inspect the training and validation loss histories. Where does training loss continue to decrease while validation loss increases? Can validation accuracy stay unchanged while validation cross entropy worsens?
Compare each validation minimum with the final epoch. How would early stopping change the parameters retained? Distinguish possible overfitting from underfitting or incomplete optimization; a larger network is not automatically an overfitted network.


architecture_results = compare_architectures(
    merged, training, validation, class_names,
    architectures=((8,), (16,), (32,), (16,16), (16,16,16), (32,32)),
    seeds=(11, 22, 33), epochs=2000, learning_rate=0.01,
)
architecture_paths = save_architecture_comparison(output, architecture_results, use_tex=True)
for run in architecture_results:
    print(run["hidden_sizes"], run["seed"], run["parameters"],
          run["best_validation_accuracy"], run["final_validation_accuracy"],
          run["best_epoch"], run["final_epoch"])
print("Architecture figures:", architecture_paths)

The accuracy figure compares the same validation observations across architectures. The loss-history figure shows seed 11 for readability; all three seeds are retained in the JSON output. Dots identify the validation minima. The range of outcomes across seeds is not a confidence interval. Selecting architectures against the same validation set is model selection, not an independent assessment of a final model’s predictive accuracy.


Document and interpret the comparison
Retain the source labels, common label mapping, exclusions, split, training settings, learning-curve results, and architecture comparisons so that the comparison can be reproduced.

Save the merged observations, training and validation IDs, mappings, and excluded observations.
Include the data-source documentation and paired learning-curve, accuracy, and loss-history figures.
Explain the main trend, its sensitivity to the seed, and at least one physical or statistical limitation. A result showing little improvement or deterioration is informative too.


record = dict(label_maps=label_maps, class_names=class_names, configuration=configuration,
              split_seed=42, merged=merged, excluded=excluded,
              training_indices=training.tolist(), validation_indices=validation.tolist(),
              results=results, architecture_results=architecture_results)
(output / "comparison.json").write_text(json.dumps(record, indent=2) + "\n")


Optional numerical data source
The numerical observations of Cano-Lozano et al. (2016) may also be considered. Their definitions and labels would require the same compatibility check before inclusion; this source is not needed for the comparison above.
